content:
Check dams are small barriers built across streams or drainage channels to slow 
down water flow and allow it to soak into the ground rather than running off 
quickly. They are especially useful in hilly or sloped terrain where water moves 
fast during monsoon season. Check dams also help reduce soil erosion and can 
recharge groundwater over a larger area than percolation pits, though they 
require more construction effort and are best suited to community-level 
implementation rather than individual households.

Contour trenches are ditches dug along the natural contour lines of sloped land 
to capture rainwater runoff and let it infiltrate into the soil. They are commonly 
used in hilly agricultural areas to prevent water from rushing downhill and 
instead hold it in place long enough to recharge groundwater and support nearby 
vegetation. Contour trenches work best on slopes with moderate gradient and are 
often combined with tree planting along the trench edges to further stabilize soil.

Percolation pits are small pits dug into the ground, filled with gravel and sand, 
that allow rainwater to slowly seep into the soil and recharge groundwater. They 
are most effective in areas with permeable soil like sandy or loamy soil. A typical 
percolation pit is 1-2 meters deep and 1 meter wide, and can be built at low costusing local materials. They work best when placed near rooftops or paved areas 
where rainwater runoff collects.
